messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fatima is an eighty-year-old widowed woman of Lebanese descent who has spent the better part of five decades working as a social worker, accompanying families through some of the most difficult passages of their lives. She came to the clinic three months ago, referred by her own physician after she disclosed, almost incidentally, that she had not left her apartment in weeks. What brought her to that point began four years earlier, when her youngest son, Karim, was admitted to the intensive care unit with a sudden and catastrophic cardiac event. For eleven days, Fatima sat beside his bed as machines breathed for him, as nurses adjusted the drips that ran into his arms through needles she could not look away from, as the unit filled with the particular sharp, chemical smell of antiseptic that she had never before found anything but neutral. Karim survived, but something in Fatima did not recover in the way she had expected.

In the months that followed his discharge, she began to notice that the world had become threaded with reminders she could not control. Walking past a pharmacy, she would glimpse a display of syringes behind the counter and feel the ICU snap back into her body before her mind had time to register what was happening — a wave of terror and grief so complete it had no image attached to it, only sensation and weight. The smell of antiseptic, encountered in a supermarket cleaning aisle or on a neighbor's hands, produced the same effect: the memory forced itself forward without invitation, arriving not as a coherent recollection but as an overwhelming emotional flood, the grief of those eleven days arriving whole and unannounced. These intrusions, in turn, deepened her conviction that she was permanently broken. She had come to believe that the woman who had sat with hundreds of grieving families and held their suffering with professional steadiness no longer existed — that what the ICU had left behind was someone diminished, someone who had failed her son by feeling so helpless when it mattered most.

That belief — that she had acted in ways that violated who she understood herself to be, that she had stood at her son's bedside paralyzed rather than competent — sharpened her sensitivity to anything that might confirm it. She found that when her mind turned toward the appraisal that she was permanently damaged, it also turned toward the memory itself, replaying not images but the texture of helplessness, which in turn made the triggers feel more potent and more present. Conversations about loss, which her professional life had once made routine, became unbearable. When colleagues or clients spoke of someone losing a loved one, the words functioned as an immediate conduit back to the ICU, and the grief on recall was so overwhelming that she began to find reasons to leave the room. Over the course of a year, she stopped attending case conferences. She began conducting fewer home visits. She told herself she was managing her caseload differently, but what she was doing was contracting.

She tried, with great discipline, to push the memories away when they surfaced — a strategy that seemed logical but that left her feeling more exhausted and more certain that she had no real control over her own mind, which only reinforced the sense of permanent damage. Avoiding hospitals and ambulances became non-negotiable; she arranged for a neighbor to accompany her to her own medical appointments, then stopped attending those as well. The decision to stop going out altogether followed gradually, the way a door closes in increments. By the time she presented to the clinic, she had not seen a client in person in two months, and her supervisor had gently indicated that her continued employment was uncertain. This occupational consequence landed heavily — Fatima had defined herself through her work for fifty years, and its loss felt like confirmation of everything she feared about herself.

What finally brought her to seek help was a phone call from Karim himself, who noticed during a visit that her apartment smelled stale and that she flinched when he mentioned a friend's hospitalization. She is most afraid, she told the intake clinician quietly, that she will never be the person she was. What she is hoping for, she added after a pause, is simply to be able to sit with someone else's pain again without drowning in her own.
